catalog_quote: Except for the few CV words in the language, which are H, the contrast has to do with how many H tone moras occur at the left edge of the word: Pattern A words have one H mora, all subsequent moras being L. In most cases, pattern B words have two H moras, any and all subsequent moras being L. The one complication concerns pattern B words which begin CVCVV: instead of having an initial H-HL tonal pattern, with a drop on the second mora of the CVV syllable, both syllables are H ... (i) There are only two possible tone patterns on a word of any given syllable structure; (ii) The two tone patterns are calculated from the left edge of the word. ... In no case is a H tone found anywhere beyond the second syllable of a word. ... It should be noted that we have not seen any need to recognize a stress contrast. audit.reasoning: Quote check: every fragment of the deciding quotation and the domain quotation is verbatim in the extracted text we hold of Hyman & Kobepa (PhonLab 2012 pp.128, 130-131, 132, 136) at the stated locators. Deciding source: a dedicated tone/prosody article (2012/2013) by Hyman with native-speaker co-author Kobepa, which reviews and resolves the contradictory earlier primaries; it is the best available description. Held older primaries agree or do not conflict: Steltenpool 1969 dictionary intro (p. x) treats Ekagi as a tone language with pairs didi/didi, ii/ii; Drabbe 1952 p.6 explicitly declines to call the phenomenon 'klemtoon' and gives tonal minimal pairs; the 1996 Indonesian Fonologi Bahasa Ekagi (pp.30-31, 48-49) posits stress+length+tone as three suprasegmentals with 'generally penultimate' stress, but it is a shallow inventory whose 'stress' pairs ([ʔa.ni] vs [ʔani]) look like the same A/B t

sources.quote: 'Mee exhibits some interesting tonal alternations, as analyzed by Hyman and Kobepa (2013) and Worbs (2016). Since the Mee tonal system has been described extensively elsewhere, we will not focus on tone in this paper, and our transcription omits tones. Mee allows (C)V(V) syllables.' No mention of word stress anywhere in the paper; speakers are Paniai and Tigi dialect.

sources.note: Catalog record (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; Drabbe 1949 adds no placement statement, only the note that syllable 'toon' is marked with a grave accent. The Moni part of the same article (sections 13ff, pp. 429-444, village Kugapa) says only 'De klinkers zijn dezelfde als in Ekari' and has no accent statement either.
